Pele Yoetz 223:23: And behold, the great fence against coming to strife at the time of judgment is to fulfill the saying of the Tanna who said (Avot 1:6), “Judge every person favorably” — he should not judge his fellow unfavorably, thinking he wishes to rob, plunder and exploit him. And even if he sees him denying it to his face, he should consider that perhaps he forgot and it seems to him that the truth is with him. And even if it is clear to him that his fellow is a liar, a robber, and a schemer, and he too multiplies words and speaks harshly, harsh words, cursing and reviling — it is the glory of a man to overlook an offense, and he should not answer the fool according to his folly (Proverbs 26:4), but rather a soft tongue breaks a bone, and he should give his cheek to the one who strikes him so that he be sated with disgrace, and say to him, “My brother and my friend, there is no need for such words; let us speak our words with respect, for God stands,” etc., “in the midst of the judges He judges” (Psalms 82:1).
Pele Yoetz 223:24: And let the litigants and all the people of the community picture that the judge who is in office in their days is Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, and as though standing before him, in accordance with the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, that Yiftach in his generation is like Samuel in his generation (Rosh Hashanah 25b), and let them be careful of his honor and awe, and not deviate from what he tells them right or left, and not go searching afterward to go to another court to overturn his ruling, for that brings out the sword of the town and accusation and great evil. Therefore let them be satisfied with whatever the judge says, for it is so; and even if he errs in judgment and takes money from someone against the law, the Lord will repay him sevenfold, for judgment belongs to God. These are some points of the straight path for those who sit in judgment, and thereby they will increase peace, and each man will return to his place in peace. And I say as good advice that the teacher should choose to dwell in a small city, even if his sustenance is meager there, for from distress comes life for him and for them. If you have understanding, understand this.
Pele Yoetz 224:1: Matan (Gift-Giving) — “A man's gift makes room for him” (Proverbs 18:16). For when the Lord widens his boundary, how good it is for him to increase his gifts — not only to the poor and to Torah scholars, which is counted as charity, but to open his hand from time to time to every person with a fitting gift, according to what the person is and according to the blessing the Lord has given him. Thereby he increases peace, love and brotherhood, and acquires a good name for himself, and he is honored among people, and it is counted for him as a great commandment. And this is not only for Israel, but he should open his hand even to the nations of the world, in accordance with the saying of King Solomon, peace be upon him (Ecclesiastes 11:1), “Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it.” And it is already recorded in the Talmud (Yerushalmi Terumot 8:4) several stories of people who did kindness to lowly and humble men, who eventually rose to greatness — for their kingdom came after that of Adonijah, and salvation came to Israel through them. It follows that this too is counted as a commandment, fulfilling the saying of King Solomon, peace be upon him, and the words of our sages, of blessed memory. And we have already heard with our own ears, and our ancestors told us, several stories of how a gift to gentiles kept its giver alive. Therefore it is good for a man whom the Lord has graced with wealth to be generous with his money, provided he does not squander too much, but manages his affairs with judgment in such a way that it brings glory to the giver and glory to him among people.
Pele Yoetz 224:2: And one who receives a gift must be very careful to discern the giver's true mind, so that his eye not turn evil toward giving it and he does so only out of embarrassment — for then the recipient stumbles into the sin of robbery, as explained in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 22a) and in Sefer Chasidim (section 316). And this is among the things for which there is no remedy, as they said regarding one who eats from a meal insufficient for its host (Rambam, Hilchot Teshuvah, ch. 4, halachah 4). And the great fence is not to demand a gift from anyone verbally, even if it appears to the eye that he gives with a whole heart, for one should not judge by appearance alone, since not every person and not every occasion is the same, and one must be wary.
Pele Yoetz 224:3: Likewise, a person should not set himself up to receive a fixed allowance from one man year after year, or month after month, or Shabbat after Shabbat, for he does not know what a day may bring, and perhaps a time will come when it becomes burdensome for him. Likewise, the recipient should not accept a fixed allowance, lest a time come when the giver gives out of embarrassment. And it is always good to decline until one sees that the giver gives with a generous eye, and one who trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him, and those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing. And one who is an honored and respected person should not purchase anything through an Israelite's hand; and if he does purchase, he should pay whatever the seller values it at the first time, in case there is concern that the seller might undersell it to him out of embarrassment. These are some points of the path for one who wishes to be saved from robbery. Let the wise man hear and add learning, for these are matters without fixed measure. And truly they said (Eruvin 65b), “A person is recognized by his pocket,” and “he who hates gifts shall live” [Proverbs 15:27].
Pele Yoetz 225:1: Memshalah (Governance/Authority) — We must praise the Master of all, who remembered us in our lowliness and has not left us without a redeemer, as He promised us through our father Jacob, peace be upon him (Genesis 49:10), “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes.” And in every generation and in every city there are found heads of the holy people who are close to the government and to positions of authority — blessed be He who has shared His glory with those who fear Him. And it is true that our sages, of blessed memory, taught (Avot 1:10), “And do not become overly familiar with the ruling power,” and especially in the cities of Ishmael, where being close to the government is a hair's breadth from death; but this is said so that a person not pursue honor and not seek familiarity with authority. However, if it is decreed upon him from Heaven, for the benefit of Israel — for even the head of a caravan is appointed from Heaven (Bava Batra 91b) — he must accept it, but let him do this, then, and be saved: let him precede his trouble with prayer, so that no mishap come from his hand, and let him find favor and good understanding in the eyes of all who see him, and not go about with matters too great and wondrous for himself lest the gentiles envy him, and let him not scorn any person, for there is no man who does not have his hour (Avot 4:3), especially a gentile, since their kingdoms follow after that of Adonijah. And let him consider that strength does not last forever, and let him fulfill the saying of Scripture (Ecclesiastes 7:14), “In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider” — which the commentators explained to mean: in the day of prosperity, foresee the day of adversity that is destined to come.
Pele Yoetz 225:2: Therefore, whatever is in his power to do good, let him do, whether with one who is a fellow member of the covenant or one who is not, and especially with his fellow Israelite — let his kindness and truth prevail, and let him be a source of relief and salvation for Israel through his position, and give his life to save the body and money of Israel from the hand of tyrannical gentiles. And needless to say, in a matter of danger to life, he should not rest or be quiet until he has effected a rescue, since whoever preserves a single life of Israel is as though he preserved an entire world (Sanhedrin 37a). And let him uphold the banner of the Torah and not rebel against the teacher's word, and let him rescue the exploited from the hand of his exploiter and not give aid to transgressors, but rather break the teeth of the wicked according to the Torah. Let him not rely on his own understanding, and not seek greatness, and not covet honor, and not cast off Torah and commandments from himself, in the manner of many wealthy men among the unlearned who have no fear of God before them. And let him not shame any person, and not take revenge or bear a grudge, and not hand over the money of Israel into the hands of gentiles, God forbid, for the evil of the informer is so great that they permitted killing him, even in this time; rather, let him conduct himself in the way of truth and righteous humility, and always remember, in his days of ascent, the possibility of a day of descent, God forbid, and let the day of death always be before him. All this and more should a living person take to heart in his time of greatness, so that his heart not become haughty and he not step out of line, but rather manage his affairs with judgment according to truth and righteousness, and thereby his greatness will continue and increase, and he will be beloved above and cherished below, and will find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, and happy is he in this world and it is well with him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 225:3: However, people must honor and exalt him, since the King, the King of the world, desires his honor. Moreover, it is the nature of a wealthy man to answer boldly (Proverbs 18:23), and when they do not honor him as he wishes, or anger him, the nearby inclination entices him with a double enticement to take vengeance and do whatever evil is in his power, saying, “If you do not fear me, now you shall see what I will do so that you fear me,” and he proceeds to inform on them or at least to curse and revile. It follows that one who angers him or does not honor him causes harm to himself, and moreover transgresses “you shall not place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14); therefore a person should be careful of every person's honor, and especially of one to whom honor is due, whether out of fear or out of respect.
Pele Yoetz 226:1: Milah (Circumcision) — It is known how great is the commandment of circumcision, which is considered as though one had offered his son as a sacrifice to the Lord. And if the Lord has graced him with knowing how to circumcise his own son, how good; and if not, he capable of it, he should be careful, when appointing another to circumcise his son, to explicitly say that he appoints him as a full agent, a man in his stead, in such a way that a person's agent is like himself, and it is considered as though he himself fulfilled the commandment incumbent upon him. And let him choose the most expert, wisest and most God-fearing mohel in the city, and it is a time to pray for his son that he be wise and God-fearing. And how good it would be if throughout all eight days he increases teaching in that room, and especially on the night of watching [before the circumcision], he should invite wise men as guests to study all night, or his own teacher, and pray for the child. (And if God is with me, I shall arrange a prayer text for this, with Heaven's help, and include it in my prayer book, and likewise for the mohel, the sandak, and the father of the son at the time of circumcision. Help me, O God of my salvation, for the sake of the honor of Your Name.) Likewise let him choose a good man as sandak, for all this benefits the child's soul, drawing upon him holiness, a pure heart and a right spirit. And it is good for the father of the son if he himself can be the sandak, for he is like an altar upon which his son is offered as a sacrifice, accepted for his atonement.
Pele Yoetz 227:1: Mechirah (Selling) — It is good for a man to sell his belongings and lands rather than bring himself to poverty. And how greatly have those people erred, as we have seen, who lose their fortunes and are in pressing circumstances, yet find it demeaning to sell their jewelry and household goods and lands all at once, to establish a good fund to sustain themselves and support their old age, and instead sell jewelry and vessels one at a time to eat meager bread, until in the end the fund is entirely depleted and they wander, asking, “Where is bread?” And the person who has understanding — for by knowledge the rooms are filled — should not be pained to sell his jewelry and his whole house and his lands to find rest for his soul, and should not need to resort to the gifts of flesh and blood or to borrowing from them, for their gift is small and their disgrace is great. And great is the evil of poverty, Heaven have mercy, as known from the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, and all the more so he should not rely on borrowing with interest, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Arachin 30b), “Let a man sell his daughter [into servitude] rather than borrow with interest,” which grows and grows, and in the end, if he cannot repay, he comes into the shackle of his own foot and comes through fire and water, as our sages, of blessed memory, said, and he will not cease to be poor and needy. And all the days of the poor are evil, and his sorrows are many.
Pele Yoetz 227:2: Therefore let every prudent person act with understanding, and as soon as he sees his hand faltering, let him hasten to find escape for himself with the blessing the Lord has given him in his house, perhaps there is hope, and after being sold he shall have redemption. And let him not worry about his children after him, to leave them lands and jewelry, for a person is close to himself and his own life comes first, and it is a law fixed as in Sheol — who can tell him whether his children will be good and upright? “A generation of the upright shall be blessed,” and if not, a house and wealth, an ancestral inheritance, will be of no benefit, for the wind will carry it all away. And it is fitting for children not to worry about themselves, but rather to have regard for their father and mother, and to support them in selling all that they have, and to sustain their old age with honor and spirit without so much trouble, and as a reward for this the Lord will command the blessing to be with them.
Pele Yoetz 227:3: And a bereaved woman [i.e., a woman of understanding] shall be praised, who, when she sees that her husband is in distress and pain, strengthens him with her good words and says to him, “My dear, let it not seem evil to you — take all that I have in the house to be a fund for your business, and we shall be satisfied with bread and become good [i.e., well off]. All jewelry and possessions are utter vanity, and better a dry morsel with quiet than [a house full of feasting with strife] (Proverbs 17:1), and it is better for me to see your face joyful and glad than all precious stones and pearls. Trust in the Lord, for He will never abandon you; He will widen your boundary and fill the house with the blessing of the Lord.”
Pele Yoetz 227:4: And this shall be the man's comfort, that the need to sell his vessels, garments, jewelry and lands is a comfort in his thinking that everything is decreed from Heaven, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 2a), “Every day a heavenly voice goes forth and says, ‘Such-and-such house is for such-and-such person, such-and-such field is for such-and-such person.’” And it is likewise found in the books that even such-and-such a garment is decreed to belong to such-and-such a person. These are wondrous things beyond the perfect Knower. And by this reasoning, one may accept that a man dies, and his children are left orphans and his wife a widow, Heaven have mercy. Therefore let the man rejoice and give thanks to the blessed Name that his soul is for life, and if he has caused his foot to slip for a while, it is all for his benefit and good, “as a father delights in a son” he is chastised, accepted as an atonement for him, and “those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31).
Pele Yoetz 228:1: Mamon (Money) — The laws of monetary matters are a great field. A person is recognized by his pocket, since a person's soul desires it, especially in these generations, a generation of money, and the way of a man is right in his own eyes, and he finds forty-nine grounds of leniency to purify the impure creeping thing, such as the prohibition of theft and robbery, fraud, interest, and encroachment on boundaries, and many other evils. And there is one whom the fear of the Lord has touched in his heart and who does not commit the well-known prohibited acts, but only does their equivalent, giving them a different name, calling them by such names as “profit,” “success,” “sharpness,” and “industriousness.” And a person in this age will say, “Every upright man who walks straight will strike his head against the wall and will not be able to eat even bran.” But a man who is a Jew and believes in the Lord and His holy Torah and the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory, should believe with complete faith that “he who amasses riches unjustly will forsake it in the midst of his days” (Jeremiah 17:11), and in the end will be a fool for the World to Come. And if it does not forsake him, it will be wealth kept by its owner to his own harm, and he is among those to whom He repays their enemies to their face, to destroy them, and woe to him and woe to his soul. But one who walks in integrity walks securely, and it is the blessing of the Lord that enriches, and there is no restraint upon the Lord to save, whether by much or by little. And one who reflects on this matter will find good either in this world or in the World to Come, his understanding being good, and one who trusts in the Lord, happy is he in this world and in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 228:2: And this is a great principle throughout the entire Torah, and especially in matters of money, that the nearby inclination blinds the clever and turns back the wise. And certainly those who walk in darkness, who have not seen the light of Torah, will surely make the straight path crooked, and the crooked will [seem to become] straight; it is fitting to be firm in strengthening oneself with great vigor to fulfill the saying of the Tanna who said (Avot 4:13 approx.), “And do not rely on your own understanding.” Let him seek guidance from books and from the mouths of scholars to know what he should do and the way he should walk. And let money not be considered anything in his eyes wherever there is a hint of prohibition, and let him distance himself from ugliness and from what resembles it, for it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent even for one hour, and moreover, those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.
Pele Yoetz 229:1: Memuneh (Appointed Official) — One appointed over the community must open his eyes to the community's affairs with all his heart and all his soul, and set aside his own business to deal with the community's needs, for they said (Yerushalmi Berachot 5:1), “Whoever engages in the needs of the many is as though engaged in Torah.” And he must be diligent and quick in his work — the work of Heaven — not resting or pausing until the matter is completed, and not letting a commandment that comes his way go stale (Rashi, Bo 12:17). And let them do all their deeds with righteousness and justice, in a good order and manner, to fulfill their duty to Heaven and to people. And if they cannot satisfy everyone, and empty and reckless people are found who speak wrongly against them, they should not worry or be troubled, for even Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, did not fully satisfy the people of Israel — “and the people spoke against God and against Moses” — but let them do their deeds for the sake of Heaven, and whoever wishes to err will err. And let no one say, “What is this trouble to me?” for if everyone said this, the congregation of the Lord would be like sheep without a shepherd. And great is the reward of those who engage with the community for the sake of Heaven, for the merit of their ancestors assists them and their righteousness stands forever.
Pele Yoetz 229:2: And how good and pleasant it would be if those appointed for the time would not rely on their own understanding, but rather give honor to the elders and the officers of the city, and consult with them on every matter — for salvation lies in an abundance of counselors (Proverbs 11:14) — and they would be a help to them against those who wish to oppose them. And certainly one who has understanding, even if he sees that those appointed for the time have acted according to what seems to him to be his own honor, regarding the aliyah to the Torah scroll, or the seating arrangement in the synagogue and the like, should not be strict about it, but should overlook his own traits, for the way of a man is right in his own eyes. And each one, in his own time of serving in holiness, should do what his heart desires and what seems right to him between himself and his Maker, and should not open his mouth and chirp. And thus should they establish in every city, for the betterment and settlement of the city. And even if he wishes to speak and raise his voice, let him speak his words calmly, with love and brotherhood, as one man speaks to his fellow, peace at the beginning and love at the end — this is the straight path.
Pele Yoetz 229:3: And it is a great fence to establish in every city that appointed officials be assigned year by year, rotating. And there are two great benefits to this: one, that whoever enters to serve in holiness at first finds it precious and great, standing to serve with great affection and to oversee the community's needs with all his strength, but afterward, due to the trouble and gossip of the many and the like, he wilts and his hands weaken — therefore it is good to have new ones each time. And another benefit: if the position is a great one, all the deserving men of the city will take a share in it, and each one will have benefit among them; and if it is servile and troublesome, all will share the burden of the people, and thus it will be borne by many hands, and one benefit that results is that they will not come to rail against the officials and speak wrongly against them, for [each will think] ‘They will do in their time what their heart desires, and we shall do in our time; and just as we do not wish to be spoken against, so we shall not speak against others.’ And thereby there will be love and brotherhood and peace and friendship in the city. And it is not fitting that the wealthy of the city be permanently fixed as leaders and officials forever; rather, let wealthy and poor mix, whoever has understanding, for money does not make a fool wise. And there are several reasons why it is good to appoint leaders each year, poor and wealthy men of understanding together, that they may be complete.
Pele Yoetz 230:1: Moneh (Counting) — It is known that it is forbidden to count Israelites (Yoma 22b), and what happened to King David, peace be upon him, because of this (ibid.). And it is not good what unlearned people do when they wish to know if there is a minyan for prayer and, wishing to be careful not to count Israelites, count “not-one, not-two, not-three, not-four” [substituting letters for numbers]. Would that they gain the wisdom to understand that their remedy does not help, for they still count them by sight and in their mind. And since our sages, of blessed memory, said (Derech Eretz Rabbah, ch. 5), “Judge every person as a potential robber, yet honor them like Rabban Gamliel,” it is fitting for anyone conducting business with his fellow not to rely on his trustworthiness alone, but rather to count immediately in his presence everything he gives and everything he receives; for if he wishes to count it afterward and finds it lacking, it is possible the giver will not be believed and will be suspected of wanting to rob him. And it also happens that the giver gave honestly and someone else came afterward and stole, unknown to him, and the giver would be suspected. Therefore, one who counts immediately in the other's presence is to be praised.
Pele Yoetz 231:1: Minchah (Afternoon Prayer) — The saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Berachot 6b): a person should always be careful about the Minchah prayer, for Elijah was answered only through the Minchah prayer. And through our sins, many unlearned people are lax about it and do not pray it with the congregation, and when they pray it alone, they pray only after twilight, a hurried and truncated prayer; and there are those who do not pray it at all, or pray the evening prayer twice, erroneously thinking that it is permitted to pray twice — but there is no make-up prayer except for one who erred unwittingly or was under complete duress, and the loss of profit is not considered duress; this is nothing but wickedness of heart and lack of faith. For one who believes with complete faith, as is true, that the blessed Name is the one who gives strength to do valiantly, will not believe that one who shortens his service will increase the honor of his house, and that one who serves his [regular] work for that reason will diminish his portion — heaven forbid to even mention it. And woe to those found not praying at all. Woe to people from the Day of Judgment and the Day of Reckoning, for now, through our sins, we have neither Temple nor anything else, and we lack all good, and this [prayer] is almost our entire service to our Creator, and this is our whole unity — that we pray morning, afternoon, and evening — and if even this is lacking, what are we and what is our life, and why should we fall short of the gentile nations who boast of their idols, many of whom leave their business and go to their houses of worship?
Pele Yoetz 231:2: And there are those whom the fear of the Lord has touched in their hearts and who rise early to the synagogue to pray the morning prayer. And Rabbi Moshe di Lonzano already wrote about this in these words: “If you are honest, you shall be tested by this: whether you also come to pray the Minchah prayer; and if not, by Pharaoh's life, you are spies, and the reason you rise early to the synagogue is that at that hour the shop is closed and no one comes in or out, but at the time of Minchah prayer, when the shop is open and the shopkeeper is extending credit, then money is considered more important in your eyes than the service of the blessed Name.”
Pele Yoetz 231:3: And there are those who do not rise early for the morning prayer, since they love to sleep the sleep of morning, and “you were compelled by the duress of sleep” — but this is not considered duress, and it does not exempt them from the Day of Judgment, for God will say, “If you seek it as silver, then you will understand the fear of the Lord” (Proverbs 2:3-5), as is known. But at least, would that they gain wisdom to come pray in the synagogue, for they said (Berachot 6a), “A person's prayer is heard only in the synagogue.” And let them also be careful about the Minchah prayer, for there is no duress of sleep, so that they may have some remedy — but if in the morning they fear the duress of sleep and in the evening the duress of business, what will become of prayer, and what will they answer on the Day of Reckoning? Were they created only to sleep and do business? And if this is how a servant of the Lord behaves, unable to set aside even two hours out of twenty-four for His service, this is shame and disgrace and cause for humiliation and wrath, Heaven have mercy.
Pele Yoetz 231:4: And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Kiddushin 20a) that once a person commits a transgression and repeats it, it becomes as though permitted to him. And if you ask a person how much it is worth to pray Minchah and Ma'ariv with the congregation, given that there are several commandments that follow and accompany them, he will answer that they are beyond value — and yet he abandons them for a small monetary gain which, by outward appearance, he judges to be a profit at that hour, which is utterly and manifestly false; for if he does profit and the way of the wicked prospers, it is the deception of the inclination, and in the end he sees no sign of blessing, and he loses more than he gains. And those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing, and the blessing of the Lord enriches (Proverbs 10:22) — this is a clear truth agreed upon by everyone in the world. But habit becomes nature, and it becomes as though permitted, to the point that through our sins many unlearned people choose to sit in the marketplaces, streets, and idle gatherings, and their souls have no desire to come to the synagogue to pray. And likewise regarding Torah study and all commandments, this is a great principle: one who accustoms himself to walk in the way of the good, the habit becomes his nature; and if one day he happens to have an impure occurrence and does not do that good deed, even if it is a matter of piety [not obligation], it will seem to him as though that day he was not a Jew. And if his heart turns away, in the end it becomes as though permitted, and he goes from evil to evil. Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself, and if his inclination overpowers him and he conducts himself in a bad way, let him hasten to find escape for himself, and let it be exchanged and traded, evil for good, for only the beginnings are hard, and afterward it becomes sweet and pleasant to him, and happy is he in this world, and it is well with him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 232:1: Meni'ah (Restraint/Abstention) — There are matters in which restraint is exceedingly good, such as in any matter where there is even a one-in-a-thousand concern of a hint of transgression and no clear commandment, where sitting still and not acting is preferable. Likewise, in a place where there is concern that one might burden his fellow with his words or by sitting with him, one should be wary even of a remote concern, and fulfill the verse (Proverbs 25:17), “Let your foot rarely be in your neighbor's house.” This requires great understanding and great skill in conduct, for sometimes what seems to a person to be sweet and pleasant to his fellow is actually a painful thorn, and though his fellow shows him a friendly face, in his heart he is thinking, “When will you leave? Finish your visit and go.”
Pele Yoetz 232:2: Thus this is a great principle in all such cases: sitting still and not acting is preferable, or at least, less is better. And it is better that people desire him and his words rather than be disgusted by him, and even in matters of preaching, he should keep it brief and finish, for it is better that they say, “How brief this one is,” than that they say, “How long-winded this one is,” and all the more so in a place where they exaggerate and his words bear no fruit — he should refrain from expounding words of ethics and instead expound aggadic matters that draw a person's heart, and all similar things. These are matters without fixed measure; let the wise man hear and add learning, and manage his affairs with judgment, loving what is fitting so that he finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 232:3: And there is a very bad kind of restraint, in the manner of what is written (Proverbs 3:27), “Do not withhold good from its owners when it is in your power to do it,” and it is written (ibid. 11:26), “He who withholds grain, the people shall curse him.” Go and learn what they said about the House of Avtinas, the House of Garmu, and Hugras ben Levi, who did not wish to teach the making of the showbread and the incense and the writing of the four letters of the Tetragrammaton at once. Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 38a) that of them it is said (Proverbs 10:7), “And the name of the wicked shall rot.” It makes a person's hair stand on end. And they also said that whoever can pray for mercy on behalf of his fellow and does not is called a sinner (Berachot 12b). Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself against his inclination, and whatever good, great or small, is in his power to do, let him do, and not withhold good, and the Lord will not withhold good, and he will merit abundant goodness in this world and in the World to Come, his understanding being good.
Pele Yoetz 233:1: Mesirah (Informing) — The saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Rosh Hashanah 16b) regarding one who informs against his fellow to authorities, that his own ledger [of merits and sins] is examined first, and he is punished first. And this is a common thing on the lips of the masses, even without knowledge, at least saying, “May the Lord repay the doer of evil according to his evil.” Would that they gain wisdom to understand that the Lord told him to curse, and when the Lord is pleased with a man's ways, even his enemies make peace with him. Why should a living man complain — let him overcome his sins (Lamentations 3:39). And what benefit is there in cursing one's fellow and informing on him — he causes himself more harm than what his fellow did to him. Therefore let him sit alone and be silent, for it has been laid upon him, and let God seek out the pursued without his informing on anyone.
Pele Yoetz 233:2: And there is another kind of informing that our sages, of blessed memory, treated very strictly, to the point that they permitted killing the informer to save the victim's life — this is handing over a fellow's body or money into the hand of gentiles without permission of the court (Bava Kamma 117a; Avodah Zarah 26b). And a man who is a Jew should tremble and take hold of himself against doing this, and not destroy himself knowingly, God forbid. And it is fitting for all city leaders to keep their eyes open regarding this and to break the teeth of the wicked with all their strength and all their might, and let there be no such thing or anything like it in Israel, for the sake of the Holy One of Israel. And for this and the like, it is fitting for the men of Israel to give their lives for the sanctification of the Lord's Name, as they said (Berachot 20a) regarding the earlier generations, for whom miracles occurred because they gave their lives for the sanctification of the Lord's Name — “the zeal of the Lord of Hosts shall do this,” as Pinchas, the zealot son of a zealot, did, and the Lord called him “peace.”
Pele Yoetz 234:1: Merirut (Bitterness) — How fitting it is for a person to be embittered with bitter weeping over his sins, iniquities and transgressions, and over the many evils and troubles he has caused, both above and below — things the mouth cannot express and several exiles could not contain — and our minds cannot grasp even one part in a thousand thousand of the evil we have caused through our sins. And because of this, no one takes it to heart to be embittered with proper weeping when reciting Tikkun Chatzot and confessions. And even the person whom the fear of God has touched in his heart, and who raises his voice in weeping, his heart is not with him; and even if he strengthens himself so that his mouth and heart are in accord and wishes to shed tears like a river, they are locked to him — all this because our sins and impurity are curtains that separate us and withhold good from us. And it is fitting for us to be firm in strengthening ourselves with great vigor to be embittered first over the fact that our eyes have grown dim and the splendor of the Divine Presence has become distant from us, to the point that we do not recognize our own deficiency, for our hearts have become as fat as suet — for had we merited that our eyes not be blurred, it would have been fitting that as soon as we remember what we have sinned against the exalted and uplifted King, and the pain we have caused the awesome and terrible King and all the heavenly host, a fountain of tears should flow from our eyes and we should shed tears like a river, streams of water without ceasing, even more than one whose only son lies dead before him, as Rabbi Elazar ben Durdaya did (Avodah Zarah 17a) — except that we are like the dead in our lifetimes, and the flesh of the dead does not feel the scalpel (and we are like donkeys and like a horse or mule without understanding). Let all who mourn, mourn over this.
Pele Yoetz 234:2: And let a person strengthen himself to think thoughts fitting to the occasion, matters that stir the heart — at a time of joy, joy; at a time of sadness, sadness. In any case, let him raise his voice and create outward arousal: at a time of joy, a voice of song and thanksgiving; at a time of sadness, let him raise his voice in weeping and stir himself as much as he can. And let him precede with prayer before the Lord that He help him and be with his heart and his mouth to do every single thing properly, as is fitting — how good is a word fitly spoken. And the Lord will not withhold good. And it is written (Ecclesiastes 3:1), “There is a time for every desire” — at a time of joy, joy; at a time of sadness, sadness. And one who mixes and confuses one with the other brings on the evening improperly [a wordplay]; rather, let him turn to each thing in its proper time, and let his heart know its own bitterness, and let no stranger intrude on its joy.
Pele Yoetz 235:1: Metikut (Sweetness) — How sweet is honey! One whose tongue speaks gentle words and whose palate is full of sweetness — such a man finds the spirit of the Omnipresent and the spirit of humankind at ease with him, his words are heeded, and he increases peace with every person, with his wife and the members of his household, for a soft answer turns away wrath (Proverbs 15:1). And especially in these generations, when people do not accept authority, the wrathful person achieves nothing but his own wrath, and would that people listen to the voice of those who speak gently with pleasant conversation and abundant affection, as they explained on the verse (ibid. 9:8), “Rebuke a wise man and he will love you” — that one should say to him, “You are wise,” etc., “and such a thing does not befit you.” In this manner should the rabbi conduct himself with the people of the city, and one person with another, and a father with his children, and a husband with his wife; and even if they treat him harshly and speak harshly to him, let him answer with a gentle tongue and sweet lips and a smiling face, and thereby he gives his cheek to the one who strikes him, so that he be sated with disgrace, while he does his own part, as it is written (ibid. 25:15), “And a soft tongue breaks a bone.” This is a great principle, a remedy for life, good for Heaven and good for humanity, good for this world and good for the World to Come. Happy is the man who does this, for he is a vessel that holds blessing and peace.
Pele Yoetz 236:1: Melamdei Tinokot (Teachers of Children) — If teachers of children act with faithfulness, how good is their portion, for of them it is said (Daniel 12:3), “And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament.” But this requires great effort and diligence from morning until evening, and I fear there is no righteous man on earth who performs this work perfectly, as is proper, and whose soul is clear of robbing the many, for they said in the Talmud (Bava Batra 8b) that Rav Shmuel bar Shilat had a garden and did not see it for thirteen years [being too occupied with teaching]. And likewise they said (Ta'anit 23b) of Abba Chilkiyah, who was a day-laborer and did not return a greeting so as not to waste even a moment's worth of speech from his employer's work. And who is so clear of guilt that he never dozes, never sleeps, never turns aside for anything, and is engaged only in his work all day? Whoever fears the word of the Lord and is concerned for his soul, lest he be included, God forbid, among those of whom it is said, “Cursed be he who does the Lord's work deceitfully” (Jeremiah 48:10), should explicitly stipulate with the parents that they permit him to oversee his household's affairs and to rest and sleep a little during the summer days and the like, so that he may have some remedy, and let him not be accused, “With our own lives we bring our bread,” for it is better for a person to be cast into hunger than [to sin], for all that a man has he will give for his life. In any case, whatever is in his power to do, let him do, and let him not waste a moment in idleness, but labor with all his strength, by the sweat of his brow, to teach them effectively.
Pele Yoetz 236:2: And study is not the essential thing (Avot 1:17), but rather Torah study combined with worldly occupation is fitting (ibid. 2:2), and “the way of life is the reproofs of instruction” — all the laws of proper conduct and all the applicable laws and reasons for the commandments; and they should be accustomed and expert in leading prayer, and in reciting the blessing for grooms, the blessing for mourners, the blessing for the host, and the like, in such a way that they become capable men. And they should advance in their studies gradually, for one who advances without gradual progression will surely fall and it will not succeed. And they should not heed fathers who have neither knowledge nor understanding, who wish their sons to advance immediately, step by step, and study Talmud, for a building without a foundation will be carried away by the wind.
Pele Yoetz 236:3: And this is the order of study: first, they should be accustomed to read the Bible fluently with its vowel points and cantillation marks, each word properly pronounced; and afterward they should learn the vernacular in all the verb conjugations, so that they know how to speak both in the Holy Tongue and in the vernacular in any book they open, and not err in their language. And he should teach them the entire Bible with understanding, and in everything they study from which an ethical lesson can be drawn, he should tell them. And with the rod of his tongue he should rebuke them for sin and for their childish behaviors, and if he needs to strike them, he should not strike them with a heavy, cruel blow, but strike them lightly with compassion, for “the obedient one obeys,” and “a rebuke enters more into a man of understanding [than a hundred blows into a fool]”, and “better is open rebuke than hidden love” expressed with a soft tongue (Proverbs 27:5). And he should accustom them to study Rashi's commentary, at first in a simple manner, and once they are accustomed, he should deepen it for them gradually, and add more Torah for them. And his eyes should be open over them to distance them from every sin and from every bad trait, and that they be complete in every kind of perfection and accustomed to good and upright traits, and especially that they be modest and careful of everyone's honor. And he should guide them with the traits of the wise and distance them from the traits of the boorish. And let him pour out his soul before the Lord that He help him so that the offshoot of his planting, the work of his hands, be a glory, with no breach and no going out [in disgrace], and thereby he fulfills his duty to Heaven and to people, and they will say, “Happy is he who raised this one, one of the great ones of holiness.” And the teacher must treat all equally and not favor the wealthy, and should be careful with the sons of the poor, for from them Torah goes forth (Nedarim 81a). These are some points of the straight path fitting for a teacher of children to conduct himself by. Let the wise man hear and add learning, and rejoice in his students in this world and delight in them in the World to Come, for there is no joy in the world greater than this.
Pele Yoetz 236:4: However, the people of the community are also obligated to keep their eyes open regarding the community's servants, and especially the teachers, who are engaged in the work of Heaven, and not to be overly critical of them, and to forgive them if their work is not done so properly, and the teachers should not be punished on their account. In any case, they should rebuke them to their face, but without anger and without harsh words, only with pleasant speech and a sweet palate, with love, as one man speaks to his fellow.
Pele Yoetz 236:5: And this is the trait of a good person, to speak his words even to his hired worker and gatherer, even if he is a gentile, and certainly to teachers, cantors, and beadles, whose distress, pressure, toil and burden are demons to them, since they serve the many who cannot all be satisfied, for this one says one thing and that one says another. And the servants must bear it all and be among those who are insulted, of whom it is said (Judges 5:31), “And may those who love Him be like the sun rising in its might.” And let them learn from Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, who bore with Israel and never fully satisfied them. But the people should be careful not to embitter them with harsh words, rebukes, and disgrace, for the Lord will plead their cause and demand their disgrace.
Pele Yoetz 236:6: And they must also keep their eyes open to provide their livelihood sufficient for their needs, in cash, week by week. And they should appoint teachers according to the children's needs, so that there are not too many children and too much material for one teacher. And they should have a designated, settled place so that they can do their work properly. And they should not worry about excessive expense, for this commandment is greater than the building of the Temple (Shabbat 119b), and it is fitting that it protect them, saving them from every trouble and distress and bringing them blessing.
Pele Yoetz 237:1: Mitah (Death) — Let the living take to heart matters of death, and especially when he sees that the wise die together with the fool and the ignorant who perish, let him take to heart that the cup of death will pass over him too. And how good it is to be present at the bedside of the sick and at the moment the soul departs, and to see with his own eyes some of what a person's soul undergoes at the time the soul departs, and to recognize the signs that our sages, of blessed memory, spoke of in the holy Zohar, true and just. And they already said (Ramban, Sha'ar HaGemul) that if a person were to suffer all the days of his life afflictions like those of Job, and more, all of it would be as nothing compared to what he undergoes at the time of death, and what he undergoes at the time of death is as nothing compared to what he undergoes afterward. And when he sees weeping, eulogies, and burial preparations, let him take to heart what a person is and what the end of flesh and blood is, and that his own end too will be to be forsaken, and they will eulogize him, and those who draw water will draw for him, and those who bury will bury him in an area of one square amah, there shall be his grave, and everyone will hurry to cover him with earth, and afterward they will leave him like a lone shrub in the desert, dealing with his own judgment, harsh judgments, bitter as wormwood and gall — yet his own flesh will feel pain and his own soul will mourn for him. These things and the like should be a constant reminder before his eyes, and thereby he is assured that he will not sin and that he will fulfill every good thing, in accordance with the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Berachot 5a): a person should always incite his good inclination against his evil inclination, etc., until he remembers for himself the day of death. It follows that remembering the day of death is more helpful than anything else for subduing the evil inclination.
Pele Yoetz 237:2: And let a person not say, “There is yet a vision for the appointed time; I am young and vigorous as cedars,” and let the evil inclination say, “Rejoice, young man, in your youth,” and “when the days of old age come, you will return to your Creator” — rather, answer it: death travels the world among young men and youths, and death does not delay, and our own eyes see a healthy, strong young man suddenly meet his doom — today he is here and tomorrow he is not, and his place will no longer recognize him. And how precious are the words of Rabbi Eliezer, who used to say (Shabbat 153a), “Repent one day before your death” — let him repent today, lest he die tomorrow, and thus all his days are spent in repentance.
Pele Yoetz 237:3: And through our sins, death is forgotten from the heart, and no one takes it to heart, and there are those who, even at the moment the dead lie before them, do not humble their uncircumcised hearts, for the enemy — the evil inclination — has overpowered them and hardens their hearts so that they fall into evil. And they already said (Eruvin 19a) that the wicked do not turn back even at the very gate of Gehinnom. But the understanding man's heart trembles within him, and terrors of death constantly fall upon him, and he improves his deeds, corrects his ways, and puts his affairs in order, and thereby he merits a good name better than fine oil, and “the day of death is better than the day of one's birth” (Ecclesiastes 7:1, and Midrash Rabbah there), and when he departs from this world, it is as one who goes to a wedding feast.
